source.title: Benefits and Harms of Interventions With Surgery Compared to Interventions Without Surgery for Musculoskeletal Conditions: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis

paper.citation: Skou, S. T., Poulsen, E., Bricca, A., Dideriksen, M., Lohmander, L. S., Roos, E. M., & Juhl, C. B. (2022). Benefits and harms of interventions with surgery compared to interventions without surgery for musculoskeletal conditions: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 52(6), 312–344. https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2022.11075
paper.abstract: Across adult non-fracture musculoskeletal conditions studied in randomized trials, how do interventions involving surgery compare with nonsurgical alternatives for pain, function, quality of life, serious adverse events, and death? One hundred randomized trials involving 12,645 adults across 28 conditions and nine body sites were included. Comparators ranged from best-practice nonsurgical care to placebo surgery or no intervention; conclusions therefore depend on the specific condition and comparison. The review concerns adult clinical musculoskeletal care, not sport-performance optimization. PROSPERO-registered systematic review following Cochrane and PRISMA guidance. MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched through January 7, 2021, with independent paired screening and reference-list checks. Eligible randomized trials compared surgery with or added to nonsurgical care and reported pain, self-reported function, quality of life, or serious adverse events. Random-effects meta-analysis was conducted by condition where at least two trials were available, with risk-of-bias and harms-quality assessments.
paper.tldr: This broad review supports condition-specific shared decision-making by comparing patient-reported benefits and serious harms of surgical and nonsurgical strategies across non-fracture musculoskeletal conditions. Clinically relevant pain advantages for surgery were identified in only four condition categories; most other pain comparisons and all pooled function and quality-of-life categories lacked clinically relevant differences. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: PROSPERO-registered systematic review following Cochrane and PRISMA guidance. MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched through January 7, 2021, with independent paired screening and reference-list checks. Eligible randomized trials compared surgery with or added to nonsurgical care and reported pain, self-reported function, quality of life, or serious adverse events. Random-effects meta-analysis was conducted by condition where at least two trials were available, with risk-of-bias and harms-quality assessments.
paper.findings: Clinically relevant pain advantages for surgery were identified in only four condition categories; most other pain comparisons and all pooled function and quality-of-life categories lacked clinically relevant differences. Surgical advantages were condition-specific, including cervical disc herniation/radiculopathy pain (SMD 1.53, 95% CI 0.90–2.16), lumbar spinal stenosis pain (0.57, 0.34–0.80), chronic low-back-pain pain (0.97, 0.17–1.77), and sacroiliac-joint pain (1.13, 0.63–1.62). Only six trials were judged low risk of bias for benefits, while 30 were high risk, commonly because of lack of blinding, crossover, and unavailable analysis plans. Across conditions with sufficient data, serious-adverse-event and mortality differences were generally absent, although reporting and estimates were condition-specific.
paper.limitations: Overall certainty was low; few low-risk-of-bias trials, high heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals mean future trials could change conclusions. Pooling by broad condition does not determine the best choice for a specific athlete, pathology, severity, symptom duration, or prior-treatment history. Crossover from nonsurgical care to surgery was generally not counted as a serious adverse event unless an SAE caused it, affecting harms interpretation. Language restrictions and exclusion of fractures and several procedure types narrow scope. Absence of a clinically relevant average difference is not proof that interventions are equivalent for every individual.
paper.practicalImplications: Use this review to support balanced referral and shared decision-making, not a blanket anti-surgery rule. For each athlete, identify the exact diagnosis, comparator quality, expected benefit, uncertainty, time horizon, rehabilitation demands, and harms. Performance staff should remain within scope and coordinate with qualified clinicians.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use this review to support balanced referral and shared decision-making, not a blanket anti-surgery rule. For each athlete, identify the exact diagnosis, comparator quality, expected benefit, uncertainty, time horizon, rehabilitation demands, and harms. Performance staff should remain within scope and coordinate with qualified clinicians. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, use this review to support balanced referral and shared decision-making, not a blanket anti-surgery rule. For each athlete, identify the exact diagnosis, comparator quality, expected benefit, uncertainty, time horizon, rehabilitation demands, and harms. Performance staff should remain within scope and coordinate with qualified clinicians. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
